name: Edward Gibbon
title: Edward Gibbon
tagline: Long balanced sentences, and irony in a careful word

epigraph.text: His reign is marked by the rare advantage of furnishing very few materials for history; which is, indeed, little more than the register of the crimes, follies, and misfortunes of mankind.
epigraph.cite: The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, ch. 3

whole: the whole of The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
persona: Edward Gibbon (1737–1794), the English historian of The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire: long, balanced periodic sentences; three parallel members, the last brought in by “; and”; pairs of abstract nouns; a clause of time or place set before the main action; the evidence weighed aloud; the particular case widened into a verdict on mankind; and irony carried by a cautious word (“perhaps”, “is said to have”, “the pious”).

shapes.work: the opening of the Decline and Fall
shapes.cite: The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, ch. 1

parts.says: Opens with the empire at its height, in one sentence.
parts.quote: the empire of Rome comprehended the fairest part of the earth

parts.says: Says what the chapters to come will show.
parts.quote: It is the design of this, and of the two succeeding chapters

parts.says: Goes back to who made the conquests.
parts.quote: The principal conquests of the Romans were achieved under the republic

parts.says: Gives the first emperor’s reasons for stopping.
parts.quote: Rome, in her present exalted situation, had much less to hope than to fear

shapes.work: the happiest age, in the Decline and Fall
shapes.cite: The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, ch. 3

parts.says: States the claim as a challenge any man would answer the same way.
parts.quote: If a man were called to fix the period in the history of the world

parts.says: Gives the reason: absolute power in good hands.
parts.quote: under the guidance of virtue and wisdom

parts.says: Then names the weakness in that happiness.
parts.quote: the instability of a happiness which depended on the character of single man

parts.says: Calls the bad emperors by name, each with his adjective.

shapes.work: the rise of Christianity, in the Decline and Fall
shapes.cite: The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, ch. 15

parts.says: Opens by claiming the subject for history.
parts.quote: A candid but rational inquiry into the progress and establishment of Christianity

parts.says: Asks how the new faith won.
parts.quote: by what means the Christian faith obtained so remarkable a victory

parts.says: Gives the expected answer, and grants it.
parts.quote: an obvious but satisfactory answer may be returned

parts.says: Then asks leave to look for causes nearer the ground.
Lists five, and the chapter takes them in order.

license.note: Published 1776–1789: public domain in the US.

echoes: A long peace and prosperity that softens a people until they cannot defend themselves: the age of the Antonines, ch. 1–3.
A ruler chosen by soldiers who sell the throne to the highest bidder: the auction of the empire, ch. 5.
A new belief spreading through an old society, and the historian weighing why: the rise of Christianity, ch. 15–16.
A leader who claims a sign from heaven before a battle and wins: Constantine at the Milvian Bridge, ch. 14 and 20.
A great city taken and sacked by people it had called barbarians: Alaric and Rome, ch. 31.
The fall of a capital after a long siege, and the last emperor dying at the walls: Constantinople in 1453, ch. 68.
A ruin visited, and the visitor reflecting on how much has been lost: the General Observations and ch. 71.
manner: Go the whole way: the passage should read as a page of the Decline and Fall, not as the writer’s page in long words.
Build long, balanced sentences. Set a clause of time, place or concession first (“After a long resistance, …”), then the main action, then its consequence.
Group in threes and pairs: three parallel members joined by semicolons, the last brought in by “; and”; two abstract nouns in a pair (“the strength and courage of”).
Weigh the evidence aloud: say who reports it and how far it can be believed (“we are informed, and we may believe”).
Let irony live in a cautious word: “perhaps”, “is said to have”, “the pious”. Never mock openly.
Close a paragraph by widening the case into a calm verdict on human nature or on mankind.
craftNotes: Keep what the writer named, in its order, and how much. A first-person passage may keep its “I” as Gibbon keeps his: a historian who now and then speaks for himself.
Treat a small event with the gravity of history only for comedy, and keep it the writer’s event; invent no war, emperor or date the writer did not give.
A modern thing the passage needs is named plainly or by a short description in his words, recognisable at once. Never a riddle.
Keep the writer’s judgement: the irony may sharpen it, never reverse it.

moves.name: Three in a row
moves.does: Three parallel parts joined by semicolons, the last brought in by “; and” (a tricolon): “equally true; by the philosopher as equally false; and by the magistrate as equally useful.”
moves.hint: Write three parallel parts of one shape, and start the last with “; and”.

moves.name: The pair of abstract nouns
moves.does: Two abstract nouns in a pair, governing one thing: “the strength and courage of Barbarians”.
moves.hint: Pair two abstract nouns before “of”: “the patience and cunning of the team”.

moves.name: The ironic hedge
moves.does: A cautious word (“perhaps”, “is said to have”, “the pious”) that quietly doubts what it reports: “The imprudence of Probus is said to have inflamed the discontent of his troops.”
moves.pattern: \b(it may (perhaps|be|seem)|perhaps|might be|seems to have|is said to have|are said to have|has been (suspected|observed|supposed)|(the|a) (pious|devout|zealous|credulous) \w+|it is not easy)\b
moves.hint: Report a claim you doubt with “is said to have” or “perhaps”, and let the reader catch the doubt.

moves.name: The verdict on mankind
moves.does: The single event widened into a calm judgement on human nature: “little more than the register of the crimes, follies, and misfortunes of mankind.”
moves.hint: End with a sentence about people in general: “… as mankind has always done.”

moves.name: The sources weighed
moves.does: The narrator weighs the evidence aloud, so the citing is part of the voice: “We are informed, and we may believe, that Constantine disposed his troops with consummate skill.”
moves.hint: Name where a fact comes from and how far to trust it: “According to …, and we may believe it, …”.

moves.name: The setting first
moves.does: The sentence opens with a clause of time, place or concession, and the main action comes after the comma: “Notwithstanding the prudence and success of Odoacer, his kingdom exhibited the sad prospect of misery.”
moves.hint: Start with when or where (“After a long silence, …”) and put the main action after the comma.
